name: Dopa-responsive dystonia
aliases: hereditary progressive dystonia with diurnal fluctuation

clinicalPearls: Most often caused by autosomal dominant variants in GCH1 (GTP cyclohydrolase 1), with reduced penetrance and a female predominance; recessive forms involve tyrosine hydroxylase and sepiapterin reductase
Classic presentation is childhood-onset lower-limb dystonia causing gait disturbance, often with a striking diurnal fluctuation (symptoms mild in the morning and worsening through the day)
The defining feature is a dramatic and sustained response to low-dose levodopa, with near-complete and durable symptom control and without the motor fluctuations seen in Parkinson disease

Because the levodopa response is so characteristic and life-changing, a therapeutic levodopa trial is essential in any child or young person with unexplained dystonia or an atypical spastic-diplegia-like picture
Some patients are misdiagnosed with cerebral palsy or hereditary spastic paraplegia for years before a levodopa trial reveals the diagnosis
Later-onset presentations can mimic parkinsonism, and features may include brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response, adding to diagnostic confusion
Diagnosis is supported by cerebrospinal fluid neurotransmitter and pterin analysis and by phenylalanine loading, and confirmed by molecular genetic testing
Unlike most dystonias the disorder is eminently treatable, so recognition carries a high clinical payoff
reference.pathophysiology: Dopa-responsive dystonia is a disorder of dopamine biosynthesis. In the common autosomal dominant form, variants in GCH1 reduce GTP cyclohydrolase 1 activity, the first and rate-limiting step in producing tetrahydrobiopterin, the essential cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase. Reduced cofactor availability lowers dopamine synthesis in nigrostriatal neurons without causing their degeneration, so the deficit is biochemical rather than structural. Because the neurons remain intact, replacing the downstream product with levodopa restores near-normal dopaminergic signalling, explaining the sustained and complete response and the absence of levodopa-related motor complications.
additionalDifferentials: Young-onset Parkinson disease and other genetic parkinsonism
DYT1 and other early-onset primary dystonias
Other inborn errors of neurotransmitter metabolism
additionalInvestigations: A carefully monitored therapeutic levodopa trial to demonstrate the characteristic sustained response
Cerebrospinal fluid neurotransmitter and pterin (biopterin/neopterin) analysis
Phenylalanine loading test to assess tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism
Molecular genetic testing of GCH1 and, where indicated, tyrosine hydroxylase and sepiapterin reductase genes
Brain MRI, typically normal, to exclude structural and neurodegenerative causes
redFlags: Diurnally fluctuating dystonia in a child that has been labelled cerebral palsy without a levodopa trial
Progressive dystonia with developmental regression suggesting a broader neurotransmitter disorder
Severe generalised dystonia impairing gait, feeding, or respiration
Failure to respond to an adequate levodopa trial, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: With levodopa treatment the prognosis is excellent: most patients achieve near-complete, durable symptom control and normal or near-normal function, and the benefit is sustained for decades without the motor complications typical of Parkinson disease. Untreated, symptoms progress and cause significant disability.
pitfalls: Failing to undertake a levodopa trial in young-onset dystonia and thereby missing an eminently treatable disorder
Accepting a longstanding label of cerebral palsy or spastic paraplegia without questioning atypical features such as diurnal fluctuation
Attributing a partial or absent response to inadequate trial duration rather than reassessing the diagnosis
Overlooking the recessive tyrosine hydroxylase and sepiapterin reductase forms, which may have a more complex phenotype
